Vitthala of Pandharpur

Temple Stories

Vitthala of Pandharpur

Pundalik's devotion and the Lord who stands on a brick

In everyday English — Panduranga-Mahatmya and the Varkari tradition

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it out loud. This story is made to be told. Read slowly, as if you are sitting with everyone at home.

This is the story of a son — and of a God who knows how to wait. There is no demon here, no war. A son serves his parents, and God stands at his door and waits. Where there is service, read slowly; where God stands on a brick, read with a smile.

The yellow boxes hold the characters' own words. Change your voice a little as you speak them — Pundalik humble, the Lord sweet, the saints singing.

(Purple hints) tell you where to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader — do not read them aloud.

The green box at the end of each part — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask questions. Let the listeners speak.

The main story of this book is from the Panduranga-Mahatmya — Pundalik's devotion and Vitthala standing on a brick, found in the Skanda Purana and the Padma Purana and sung by the Varkari saints in their abhangas. Where something comes from a later or local telling, it is given separately in a note — never blended into the main story. All the sources are named separately at the end, in Where This Story Comes From.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Pundalik — a young man who lived in a village near Pandharpur. At first he paid no attention to his parents; then serving them became his whole life. He is regarded as the first devotee of the Varkari tradition.

Pundalik's parents — his old mother and father, whom Pundalik serves every day — feeding them, pressing their feet, listening to them.

Shri Krishna — the Lord of Dwarka, who comes to Pundalik's house — and stands on a brick to become Vitthala.

Vitthala (Vithoba / Panduranga) — the dark-skinned Lord, tall crown on his head, yellow dhoti, both hands on his hips, standing on a brick. The chief deity of Pandharpur.

Rakhumai (Rukmini) — Vitthala's wife. Fair-skinned, in a red saree with a gold border. She has her own separate sanctum in the temple.

Jnaneshwar — a saint of the 13th century, who wrote the Jnaneshvari in Marathi. His palanquin comes from Alandi to Pandharpur.

Namdev — a saint of the 13th-14th centuries, singer of abhangas. The first step of the temple is named after him — the Namdev Payari.

Tukaram — a saint of the 17th century, singer of abhangas. His palanquin comes from Dehu to Pandharpur.

Varkaris — devotees of Vitthala, who walk on foot to Pandharpur — singing, dancing, on the wari pilgrimage.

1 · Pundalik — The Son Who Changed · · PUNDALIK, THE SON WHO CHANGED

This is a very old story. In Maharashtra, on the banks of the Bhima river, near Pandharpur, there lived a young man named Pundalik in a village. He lived with his old parents — but he paid them no attention.

Pundalik stayed busy with his own work — his own world, his own comforts. When his mother called, he heard and ignored her. When his father spoke, he put him off. His old parents quietly did their own work, and waited for their son to change.

Then one day Pundalik set out on a journey — and on the way he met some saints and holy people. He saw them — day and night they were busy serving others. They wanted neither wealth nor fame — service itself was their joy.

One saint said to Pundalik — “Son, God is not found in temples — he is found in serving one's parents. Whoever serves his old mother and father is the true devotee.”

(Read slowly here — let what changed in Pundalik's heart be heard.)

That word settled in Pundalik's heart. He came home — and he changed. Now he rose in the morning and touched his mother's feet, fed his father, washed their clothes, pressed their feet at night. Small acts of service — every day, without stopping, without tiring.

The people of the village watched and said — “Is this the same Pundalik? He has completely changed!” But Pundalik wanted no one's praise. His service itself had become his worship.

How Pundalik changed — the tellings differ

Sridhara's Panduranga-Mahatmya (750 verses) tells in detail that Pundalik first neglected his parents and changed through the company of saints. Some tellings link his change to a pilgrimage to Kashi — there he met holy women, named in some tellings as the rivers Ganga, Yamuna and Saraswati, who washed away pilgrims' sins through their service. This book takes the main telling that is the same in all versions — first neglect, then change after meeting holy people, then daily service — and gives the other details in this separate note, never blended into the main story.

Pause and think — At first Pundalik paid no attention to his parents — then one word changed him. Can a single word really change a person? And Pundalik's service was small — feeding, pressing feet. Is worship only in great deeds — or can small daily service also be prayer?

2 · Krishna Comes · · KRISHNA COMES

Days passed. Word of Pundalik's service spread far and wide — it is said the fragrance of his devotion reached all the way to Dwarka. And one day, while Pundalik was pressing his father's feet, there was the sound of someone arriving outside his house.

Standing at the door was Shri Krishna himself — dark-skinned, crown on his head, yellow dhoti, the Vaijayanti garland around his neck. He had come to meet Pundalik.

Pundalik saw him — and bowed in his heart. But he did not get up. His hands were on his father's feet, and his work was not yet finished.

Pundalik said, sitting right there without joining his hands — “Lord, you have come — I am blessed. But my parents' service is not yet finished. Will you wait a little while? I will come at once.”

(Whisper here — Pundalik has asked God to wait!)

Krishna smiled. He was not angry — he was delighted. A son who will not leave his parents' service even before God — his devotion is true.

Pause and think — God himself came to the door — and Pundalik said, “Wait.” Was that disrespect — or was it the greatest devotion? And why was Krishna not angry — does God love a devotee's service more than his own greatness?

3 · The Lord Who Waited · · THE LORD WHO WAITED

Pundalik picked up a brick lying near the door and set it outside. “Lord, stand on this and wait — the courtyard is muddy, your feet will get dirty. I will finish my service and come at once.”

And Krishna accepted the brick. He stood upon it — both hands on his hips — and waited patiently. No hurry, no anger — only a smile and waiting.

Pundalik finished his service — he fed his father, gave his mother water, settled them both comfortably to sleep. Then he came outside and fell at the Lord's feet.

Pundalik said — “Lord, forgive me — I made you wait.”

Krishna said — “Pundalik, you did not make me wait — you gave me the dearest thing of all. Whoever serves his parents serves me. Ask, what boon do you want?”

Pundalik asked nothing for himself. He said — “Lord, stay here — in this very form, on this very brick — so that every devotee who comes here may have your darshan and find peace of heart.”

Krishna said — “So be it.” And he stayed there — as Vitthala — standing on a brick, hands on his hips, waiting for everyone. It is said he has stood there ever since — in the language of devotees, for twenty-eight yugas — and he stands there still today.

Twenty-eight yugas?

“God has stood on the brick for twenty-eight yugas” — this is the language of devotion, not a date in history. It is a way of saying that he has stood there, without moving, waiting for his devotees, for a very, very long time. This book gives it in that form — as “it is said” — and it should not be read as a year or a date. This framing also comes from the reel that prompted this book — named in the sources.

The brick and the hands on the hips

This form of Vitthala — standing on a brick, both hands on the hips — is the temple's own telling of why he looks as he does. In the tradition the name Vitthala is linked to ‘vit’ (brick) + ‘sthala’ (a place of standing) — “the one who stands on a brick”. In the sanctum at Pandharpur today, the black-stone murti about three and a half feet tall still stands in exactly this form — it is the temple's mark of recognition.

Pause and think — Pundalik asked nothing for himself — he asked God to stay for everyone. Is asking wrong — or is the way of asking also devotion? And God still stands on the brick today, waiting — for whom is he waiting? For us too?

4 · Rakhumai — Rukmini · · RUKMINI — RAKHUMAI

Vitthala does not live alone — with him is Rakhumai, that is, Rukmini — the queen of Dwarka, the wife of Shri Krishna. In Pandharpur she has her own separate sanctum, right beside Vitthala's temple, with her own darshan queue.

It is said that Rakhumai had first left Vitthala in anger — and then met him here in Pandharpur. Since then she dwells here — fair-skinned, in a red saree with a gold border, hands on her hips just like Vitthala, standing on a brick.

Devotees first take darshan of Vitthala, then of Rakhumai — or many take Rakhumai's darshan first, then Vitthala's. In the temple each has their own place, but both are one family — one story, one home.

Why did Rakhumai leave in anger?

The story of Rakhumai's coming to Pandharpur is the temple's own telling, not the main Puranic story. The popular Marathi telling says that Rukmini was upset at Shri Krishna's attention to Radha and left — and then met him in Pandharpur. This is the devotional tradition's own telling — so it is given here in a separate note, not blended into the main story. Her own separate sanctum and her own darshan queue in the temple are real.

Pause and think — In Vitthala's temple Rakhumai has her own place — her own queue, her own sanctum. Is having one's own place also love, between husband and wife? And Rakhumai left in anger — is anger also a form of love?

5 · The Temple Today · · THE TEMPLE TODAY

Today Pandharpur stands in the Solapur district of Maharashtra, on the banks of the Bhima river. Where the river bends like a crescent moon, it is called the Chandrabhaga — the moon-bent river. The main door of the temple faces this river.

In the sanctum stands Vitthala's black-stone murti — about three and a half feet tall, on a brick, hands on his hips. The old part of the temple is dated to the time of the Hoysala king Vishnuvardhana (1108–1152 CE). The first step of the temple is called the Namdev Payari — after the saint Namdev.

Four times a year comes the wari — Chaitri, Maghi, Ashadhi and Kartiki — each time on the ekadashi of the bright fortnight. The greatest of these is Ashadhi Ekadashi — then lakhs of warkaris walk on foot to Pandharpur, carrying the saints' palanquins with them. Kartiki Ekadashi is also great.

There are two kinds of darshan — mukh-darshan, in which the Lord's face is seen from a distance, and pada-sparsha darshan, in which devotees may touch Vitthala's feet — for that, a long queue forms.

On the riverbank stands a small temple to Pundalik too — the son because of whom God came here. Devotees go there as well and bow their heads.

The history of the temple

The main part of the temple is dated to the time of Hoysala king Vishnuvardhana (1108–1152 CE) — the same king who, it is said, was moved by Pundalik to build the temple of Vitthala. In later centuries the Maratha Peshwas and nobles adorned the temple again. The temple as it stands today is made of layers from many centuries — so no single date belongs to the whole temple.

Pause and think — Lakhs of people walk on foot to Pandharpur — no vehicle, no hurry — just singing and walking. Can walking itself be worship? And the first step of the temple is named after a saint — do the steps of a temple also remember people?

6 · The Saints of the Wari · · THE SAINTS OF THE WARI

Vitthala's story began with Pundalik — but it did not stop there. From the 13th century, saints sang Vitthala in their abhangas — small Marathi hymns, which are still sung in every wari today.

Jnaneshwar — a saint of the 13th century, who wrote the Jnaneshvari in Marathi — an explanation of the Gita in the language of ordinary people. His palanquin sets out from Alandi.

Namdev — a saint of the 13th-14th centuries, who sang abhangas and said that God lives not in the walls of a temple but in the heart of a devotee. The first step of the temple is named after him.

Tukaram — a saint of the 17th century, from the village of Dehu. He wrote thousands of abhangas — calling Vitthala his friend, his brother, his father. His palanquin sets out from Dehu.

With them walked more saints — Eknath, Janabai, Chokhamela — each carrying Vitthala's story from home to home in their own songs.

The saints' stories — in brief

This part does not give the saints' full life stories — those are the Varkari tradition's own tellings, and each saint has a long story of his or her own. Only what joins this book's story is given here — their palanquins, their abhangas, and their bond with Pandharpur. The dates of Jnaneshwar, Namdev and Tukaram are given by century — scholars differ on the exact years.

Pause and think — The saints called Vitthala not a king but a friend — “Mauli”, “Bapa”. Is calling God a friend also devotion? And their songs are still sung today — seven hundred years later. Are songs also like temples — which time cannot break?

The story that began with Pundalik's service still goes on today — in every wari, in every abhanga, in the feet of every devotee.

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

Main source

The main story of this book is from the Panduranga-Mahatmya — Pundalik's devotion and Vitthala standing on a brick. In the Skanda Purana it is found in two versions (about 900 verses); in the Padma Purana there is also a version of it (about 1,200 verses).

Parallel sources

The Bhima-Mahatmya of the Padma Purana and the Panduranga-Mahatmya found in the Vishnu Purana are parallel sources for this story. Where the versions differ, this book takes the telling that is the same in all of them — Pundalik's service, the brick, the waiting, and the Lord staying on.

The Varkari tradition

The compositions of the Varkari saints are the living tradition of this story — Mahipati's Bhaktalilamrita and Bhaktavijaya, Bahinabai's Pundalika-Mahatmya, and Namdev's long abhanga. In them Pundalik's story is sung.

Sridhara's Panduranga-Mahatmya

Sridhara's Panduranga-Mahatmya (750 verses) is the version in which Pundalik's early neglect and his change through the company of saints is told in detail. Prahlada Maharaj's Panduranga-Mahatmya (181 verses) belongs to the same tradition.

Twenty-eight yugas — the language of devotion

“He has stood for twenty-eight yugas” — this is the language of devotion, not a date in history. In this book it is given as “it is said”, and its own note sits in §3.

Rakhumai's story

The story of Rakhumai's coming to Pandharpur is the temple's own telling — its own note sits in §4. Her own separate sanctum and her own darshan queue in the temple are real.

The temple and the wari

The history of the temple, the four waris (Chaitri, Maghi, Ashadhi, Kartiki), the arrival of the palanquins on Ashadhi Ekadashi, mukh-darshan and pada-sparsha darshan, and the Namdev Payari — these come from the Pandharpur temple tradition and the Maharashtra Tourism Department's Pandharpur page.

The reel that prompted this book

This book was prompted by an Instagram reel — @toonpuranas, “He asked God to wait… and offered him a brick” (16 November 2026). The reel was only a pointer, not a source — every one of its beats was checked against the Puranic and tradition sources named above before it was written into this book. The reel names the Maharashtra Tourism Department's Pandharpur page (maharashtratourism.gov.in/temple/pandharpur/) as its source — that is a tourism page, not scripture.

Sanskrit manuscripts

Sanskrit manuscripts were NOT consulted for this book — the chapter-level references to the Puranas and the descriptions of the Varkari tradition were checked from web sources. That is why no verse numbers are given here.

About the pictures

In this book's pictures Vitthala is shown as he is worshipped in Pandharpur — dark-skinned, tall crown, yellow dhoti, both hands on his hips, standing on a brick. Rakhumai is shown fair-skinned, in a red saree with a gold border.
